Adage

AD-ij -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, AD; the ending sounds like the end of 'village.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Adage is a traditional saying that expresses a general truth.

Her writing teacher's favorite adage, 'show, don't tell,' was printed at the top of every assignment sheet.

Worked Example

All week, Marcus tells everyone he has won the science fair -- the judges seemed to love his volcano. At the ceremony, first place goes to a quiet girl with a solar oven. His grandmother pats his shoulder and says only, 'Don't count your chickens before they hatch.'

Grandmother's line is an adage: a traditional saying that expresses a general truth. Adages are old, short, and battle-tested -- generations kept repeating them because they kept turning out to be right. Marcus just learned this one the hard way.

How Adage Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

proverb

proverb: a short traditional saying stating a truth

saying

saying: a well-known short expression

byword

byword: a phrase everyone in a group repeats as wisdom

Antonyms

falsehood

falsehood: a statement that is untrue

absurdity

absurdity: a claim with no sense or truth in it

How Strong Is It? — saying → adage → proverb

saying vs. adage

saying vs. adage: Saying is the loosest of the three -- any short expression people repeat counts -- while an adage must carry a general truth inside it.

proverb vs. adage

proverb vs. adage: Proverb is the strongest and most official: an adage may just be a familiar old line, but a proverb has been polished by so many generations that it reads like folk law.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ad-

prefix — ad-: to, toward (Latin)

root — age

root — age: to say (Latin aio 'I say')

Put it together

Put it together: Adage comes from Latin adagium, built on ad- ('to') plus the root of aio, 'I say' -- roughly, 'something said toward' a situation. An adage is exactly that: the ready-made thing people say to a moment, the line a grandmother reaches for because a thousand grandmothers reached for it before her.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: The Latin root aio ('I say') built no other English word; adage is its lone descendant. An adagium was Rome's name for a saying kept ready to be said 'toward' a moment. That is still what an adage is: the line that gets said because generations have already proved it worth saying.

Root Check

Word Choice

An adage is a saying with mileage on it -- old, traditional, handed down: 'haste makes waste,' 'actions speak louder than words.' You met the very similar word maxim earlier in this course: a maxim is any short statement of a general truth, while an adage is specifically the old, traditional one that has been passed along for generations. Every adage could be called a maxim, but only the time-worn ones earn the name adage.
